content: The percentage of Massachusetts residents covered by health insurance significantly increased following the implementation of health-care coverage legislation. Among Hispanic respondents who completed the survey in Spanish, the largest reported increase was observed, with a 19.9% rise. Overall, the percentage of Hispanics with health insurance increased by 14.1%. The proportion of men reporting routine checkups rose by 5.1%, from 66.4% to 69.8%, while the percentage of women reporting routine checkups did not change significantly. Similarly, the percentage of respondents with chronic conditions who reported having a personal health-care provider or undergoing an annual checkup did not show significant changes after the enactment of the health-care coverage law. A broader comparison between the 2005 and 2008 BRFSS state survey results revealed that health insurance coverage among all state residents, including children and adults aged 65 years or older, increased from 89% to 97%. After the law's implementation, the proportion of respondents who reported lacking health insurance was approximately halved. The observed effects are likely attributable to the new law, although causality cannot be definitively proven due to inherent limitations in such studies. Increases in health insurance coverage can result from various factors, such as higher employment rates, reduced health insurance premiums, or the expansion of existing public health insurance programs. The analysis also highlighted increases in insurance coverage among traditionally underserved subpopulations, such as Hispanics, individuals with less than a high school diploma, and those with annual household incomes below $25,000. However, despite these increases, Hispanics continued to have the lowest health insurance coverage and the lowest percentage of individuals with a personal health-care provider compared to other subpopulations. The percentage of younger adults, whites, Blacks, and individuals with chronic diseases who reported having a personal health-care provider did not change significantly. This may be due to the need for more time to realize the effects of improved health-care access in these groups or the unequal accessibility of health-care providers for certain populations or in specific areas. The cost of a doctor visit might also play a role, but 2008 BRFSS data showed that only 6% of respondents reported being unable to visit a doctor in the past year due to cost, compared to 8% in 2006. Before the law's enactment, the proportions were 80.8% private, 14.8% public, and 4.4% other. After the law, these proportions shifted to 78.2%, 19.2%, and 2.6%, respectively.
